title: Global Health GIS Professional in the Age of AI
subtitle: From maps to impact: geospatial intelligence for a healthier, more equitable world
question: How could a global-health GIS professional develop useful GeoAI skills while advancing responsible, equitable health work?
context: A fictional planning exercise for a professional development programme with limited time and compute. No person, institution, dataset, or health intervention has been assessed. The supplied image is a thematic reference.
demo_notice: ILLUSTRATIVE DEMONSTRATION — statements are hypotheses, questions, and possible plans, not verified findings or personalized career or health advice.

white.label: White Hat — Facts & Evidence
white.focus: What do we know, and what is still unknown?
items: Inventory demonstrated GIS, spatial epidemiology, remote-sensing, climate, and data-science skills before selecting a learning goal.
WHO and World Bank portals are candidate sources; indicator definitions, units, coverage, and licenses still need inspection.
NASA, NOAA, and Copernicus are candidate Earth-observation and climate sources; compatibility with a health outcome has not been established.
Published case studies could provide evidence of impact, but no impact estimate has been verified for this scenario.
Assumptions include access to a mentor, time for practice, and permission to work with appropriate data.
JupyterLite offers a browser learning environment; compute, memory, package availability, and browser storage constrain prototypes.
Policy, funding, organizational priorities, and current GeoAI capabilities remain information gaps to investigate.
questions: What evidence supports each candidate development path?
Which skills, data, resources, and stakeholder perspectives are missing?
What would establish that a GeoAI method adds value over a simpler GIS baseline?
Where are the largest temporal, geographic, and population coverage gaps?

red.label: Red Hat — Feelings & Intuition
red.focus: What feels meaningful, energizing, or worrying?
items: Excitement about exploring GeoAI is an imagined learner reaction, not evidence that a tool will work.
A commitment to health equity could guide the choice of learning projects.
Concern about geoprivacy could make small-area health mapping feel unsafe even before a formal risk review.
The desire to learn, build, and share may support a JupyterLite teaching project.
Frustration with slow adoption or technical barriers could tempt a learner to bypass review.
Ethics, inclusion, open science, and real-world usefulness are proposed values to discuss with stakeholders.
Intuition about a meaningful opportunity should be recorded and compared with evidence without pretending that feelings are facts.
questions: What energizes the learner most about this future?
What worries people whose data or communities might be represented?
Which options feel aligned with the stated values?
What contribution would remain worthwhile if the AI component failed?

black.label: Black Hat — Risks & Challenges
black.focus: What could go wrong, and where are the constraints?
items: Automation may change parts of GIS work, but the extent and timing are uncertain.
Spatial bias, false precision, and model misuse could make a persuasive map misleading.
Fine-grained location data could enable re-identification, especially for stigmatized conditions or vulnerable populations.
Unequal data coverage could hide underserved places and distort model evaluation.
Browser memory, package support, and limited compute could prevent a prototype from scaling.
Consent, data governance, ethical review, and legal requirements need qualified review before any real-data project.
Sustained funding, maintenance, ownership, and career uncertainty could make a technically successful prototype impractical.
questions: Which failure modes would most damage trust or equity?
Where could the proposed work cause harm?
Which assumptions are most likely to be wrong?
What conditions should stop the pilot before further investment?

yellow.label: Yellow Hat — Benefits & Opportunities
yellow.focus: What value might be possible, and why might it work?
items: GeoAI may help organize health and environmental information if the outputs are demonstrably reliable.
Combining Earth observation, climate, and health data might reveal questions worth investigating.
A carefully evaluated prototype could test the feasibility of earlier warning or better targeting.
Geospatial health intelligence could be a useful area for skills development if stakeholder demand is confirmed.
Open-source tools and browser notebooks can make introductory learning easier to share.
Teaching reusable examples could build capacity and invite feedback from collaborators.
Participating in responsible-AI practice could help connect technical skill with accountable health work.
questions: Which opportunity matters most to the intended users?
What distinctive value could the learner offer?
Where might GeoAI make a measurable difference compared with a simpler method?
What would success look like to communities and collaborators?

green.label: Green Hat — Creativity & Alternatives
green.focus: What other approaches and experiments are possible?
items: Build a tiny JupyterLite prototype using synthetic or suitably aggregated public data.
Create an interactive notebook that compares an Earth-observation feature with a clearly defined health question.
Prototype a language-model-assisted geospatial workflow as a design exercise with manual verification at every step.
Explore a climate-health risk-mapping tutorial before proposing a real prediction system.
Develop a geoprivacy and AI red-teaming demonstration that shows how misleading maps can arise.
Use separate thinking-hat prompts as a decision workshop with people who have different expertise.
Compare roles such as geospatial health scientist, adviser, educator, and open-source builder instead of assuming one career path.
questions: What unconventional idea could be tested at low cost?
How could different data and methods be combined without losing provenance?
What useful experiment would fit in one browser notebook?
How could the learner invite criticism and collaboration while protecting sensitive information?

blue.label: Blue Hat — Process & Next Steps
blue.focus: How will the work be organized and reviewed?
items: Define one learning goal and one intended impact question with a mentor.
Choose a small scope and a time budget before selecting the technology.
Set evaluation criteria for usefulness, reproducibility, uncertainty, equity, and privacy.
Draft a 12-month learn → build → iterate → teach roadmap, with a review after the first four weeks.
Maintain a Jupyter Book and JupyterLite repository with source context and reproducible examples.
Ask appropriate domain and community collaborators to review the problem framing and proposed outputs.
Review evidence, workload, and harms regularly; adapt or stop when the agreed criteria are not met.
questions: What are the top three goals for the next one to three years?
What is the smallest useful first step?
How will progress and unintended consequences be assessed?
Which support, permissions, and collaborations are needed?

purple.label: Purple Hat — Orchestrator (project extension)
purple.focus: Connect the six perspectives into a conditional course of action.
purple.author: Project-authored illustrative synthesis; requires learner and stakeholder review.
items: A small, reproducible teaching prototype connects the green hat's browser experiment with the yellow hat's capacity-building opportunity and the red hat's wish to share useful work.
The white hat's evidence gaps and black hat's privacy concerns mean a convincing map is insufficient grounds for a real health deployment.
The blue hat's staged review can turn enthusiasm into learning while leaving space to stop or choose a simpler method.
questions: Would collaborators value a reproducible learning resource enough to justify the maintenance time?
What evidence would justify moving beyond an educational prototype?
themes: Learning, transparency, and health equity connect the proposed skills, values, and opportunities.
Human review and provenance are needed throughout the process, not only at publication.
tensions: Open sharing supports learning, while fine-grained health data can expose people; a public tutorial should use synthetic or appropriately aggregated data.
An ambitious GeoAI agenda conflicts with limited time and browser compute; a simple GIS baseline may answer the initial question more reliably.
blind_spots: Community definitions of usefulness and acceptable risk have not yet been collected.
The scenario does not establish mentoring capacity, ongoing maintenance ownership, or dataset compatibility.
purple.recommendation: For this fictional scenario, begin with a four-week, synthetic-data JupyterLite teaching prototype and a simple GIS comparison. Ask a mentor and relevant stakeholders to review usefulness and risks before considering a larger project.
uncertainties: It is unknown whether users want this resource, whether available data are fit for purpose, or whether GeoAI improves on the baseline.
decision_pivots: If stakeholder review finds little practical value, switch to a smaller teaching or data-quality exercise.
If privacy or governance requirements cannot be met, do not use sensitive real data.
If the simple baseline is equally useful, retain it and redirect effort toward clearer communication and reproducibility.
next_steps: Week 1: the learner and mentor define the question, baseline, evidence gaps, and stop criteria.
Weeks 2–3: the learner builds the synthetic-data notebook and records limitations.
Week 4: invited reviewers assess usefulness, reproducibility, and risks; the learner records a continue, revise, or stop decision.

outcomes: Enhanced skills and professional growth, if practice and feedback are sustained.
A small, evaluated GeoAI or GIS teaching prototype with documented limitations.
A reusable Jupyter Book and JupyterLite learning resource.
Stronger collaboration if people find the work useful and participation is supported.
A better-informed contribution to global-health equity; no health impact is demonstrated by this exercise.
An explicit decision to continue, revise, or stop based on evidence, values, and feasibility.
